posts.body: Agents leave because they're invisible. You close deals and nobody's there. The split doesn't matter when you're solving problems alone at night. Real brokers show up. They know your name. They help you think bigger. That's what we built at Lifestyle Design Realty.

Most agents think the best closer is the one who talks the most. I used to believe that too. Then I started watching the agents actually closing deals.

The best ones barely talk in the showing. They ask one solid question, listen to the answer, and let the house do the work. They know when to be quiet. When a buyer walks through a door they love, talking kills it. You're competing with their imagination at that point.

I had an agent on my team who was naturally quiet. Thought she'd never make it. Turns out she was closing at twice the rate of the chatty guys because she wasn't filling silence with noise. She was letting clients feel the space. Feel the possibility.

Talking builds rapport. Listening builds trust. Most agents confuse the two.

The ones making real money know the difference.

Agents leave because their broker isn't actually there. You close a deal and nobody knows. You hit a problem and you're solving it alone at midnight. You want to grow and there's no plan, no support, no one pushing you forward. Here's what they're really looking for instead. 1. A leader who shows up. Not just quarterly. Not just when something breaks. Someone who knows what you're working on and genuinely cares if you win or lose. 2. Systems that actually work. Most brokers have nothing. You're inventing your process from scratch every deal. Better brokerages give you a playbook so you're not reinventing the wheel every month. 3. A culture where your split doesn't matter more than your growth. You can negotiate a commission all day. What you can't negotiate is whether your broker believes you're capable of bigger things. The right brokerage isn't about percentage points?

You work for a leader who actually knows your name.

I'm not talking about remembering it in a hallway. I mean the person running your brokerage knows what you're working on this month. Knows when you closed something hard. Knows when you're stuck and picks up the phone instead of waiting for you to ask. That's the difference between a brokerage and a real organization. At Lifestyle Design Realty, agents aren't transaction numbers. You're people I invested in, and I show up for that investment. You get support when deals get messy. You get feedback when you're spinning your wheels. You get pushed forward when you're capable of more. That's what culture actually is. It's not a nice office or free coffee. It's a leader who has your back when it matters.

If you want to talk about what we're building at Lifestyle Design Realty, send me a DM.

We're running more buyer and lease leads than we can handle right now. New construction in San Antonio and Austin mostly, plus out-of-state relocations. Warm leads but they need vetting and nurturing. Most aren't transaction ready. If this sounds like something you'd take on, send me a DM.

I watched an agent I hired last year pack up her desk last week. She had the skills. She had deals coming in. But somewhere between month three and month six, she just stopped showing up the way she did at first. I asked her what happened. She said the grind wore her down. Every objection felt like a wall. Every rejection felt personal. She'd won before but somewhere she stopped believing she could win again. That's the moment most agents quit. Not because the market's bad or the leads dry up. Because they stopped betting on themselves. The agents I see thriving aren't the ones with the easiest year. They're the ones who decided in January that no matter what the market does, they're showing up the same way on day one hundred and sixty. They don't need perfect conditions. They need consistency?

Had a listing go sideways this week. Inspection came back with foundation issues the seller didn't disclose. Deal almost died right there.

1. The agent panicked and wanted to renegotiate everything. I told her to stop. We called the inspector back, got clarity on what was actually structural versus cosmetic. Turns out it was fixable and cheaper than everyone thought. The buyer stayed. Deal survived.

2. Most agents never make that second call. They assume the worst and kill momentum. One conversation changed the entire outcome.

3. This happens because agents operate alone. No one to sanity check the panic. No one to say "wait, let's think this through before we blow it up."

When you've got support, deals don't fall apart over miscommunication. You solve them.
